analysis.one_liner: Treats companies that reincorporate offshore to avoid U.S. taxes as domestic corporations again.
analysis.headline: The bill to re-tax companies that moved offshore died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip the tax benefits of "corporate expatriation" — when a U.S. company sets up a paper headquarters in a foreign country, usually a tax haven, to lower its U.S. tax bill. Companies doing this would be treated as American corporations for tax purposes, and executives would have to tell shareholders what an expatriation would cost them. As a sweetener, it also raises the amount of equipment small businesses can write off immediately each year, from $25,000 to $75,000 through 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers generally, because companies that renounce their U.S. incorporation to cut taxes would keep paying U.S. income tax instead of shifting the burden onto individuals. Shareholders gain new required disclosure about what an expatriation deal would do to their stock, including the estimated tax benefit to the company. Small businesses gain a larger immediate write-off for equipment purchases through 2007.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines the acquiring company in a corporate expatriation transaction — where a nominally foreign company ends up more than 80% owned by the U.S. company's former shareholders — as a domestic corporation for tax purposes, so the deal no longer lowers U.S. taxes.

Applies a stricter 50% ownership test when the foreign company is just a paper shell with little real business activity in its home country and its stock trades mainly in the United States, and covers similar moves through partnerships.

Requires companies to give shareholders a separate disclosure with any proxy statement for an expatriation deal, covering how many employees and what share of assets would move abroad, how shareholder rights would change, the capital-gains tax hit to holders, and the estimated tax benefit to the company — and to report each shareholder's vote on the deal to the SEC.
Temporarily raises the Section 179 expensing limit to $75,000 and the phaseout threshold to $325,000 (through 2007), letting small businesses deduct more equipment cost immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that have completed or plan expatriation deals, which would owe U.S. income tax as domestic corporations — retroactively for deals after September 11, 2001, and for taxable years after 2003 even for deals dating back to the end of 1996. The federal Treasury gives up some revenue from the larger small-business expensing break.

drawbacks.text: The tax rules apply retroactively — to expatriation deals completed after September 11, 2001, and for taxable years after 2003, back to deals completed after December 31, 1996 — so companies and their shareholders who lawfully finished such transactions would face new taxes on past deals.

The small-business expensing increase is a straight revenue cost through 2007, a tax cut attached to a loophole-closing bill, which its backers would have to acknowledge reduces the revenue the main provision raises.
The new proxy disclosures and SEC vote reporting would impose compliance costs on companies considering expatriation, on top of the tax change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provision is a genuine loophole-closer: it would stop U.S. companies from cutting their tax bill by reincorporating in a low-tax country while keeping their business and stockholders in the United States, and the disclosure rules give shareholders real information about what a deal would do to them. The main honest objection is retroactivity — companies that completed expatriations before the bill's introduction would owe tax on past transactions, which raises fairness concerns even though the targeted deals were designed mainly to reduce taxes. The small-business expensing sweetener muddies the revenue picture but is modest and temporary.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 108th Congress ended with no vote and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Senator Evan Bayh introduced the Corporate Tax Fairness and Shareholder Rights Act of 2003 on March 4, 2003.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no markup, no vote was ever reported — and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that had already expatriated or wanted to were better off: the bill never advanced, so they kept the ability to renounce U.S. incorporation and the resulting tax savings, and no retroactive tax rules ever applied to past deals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies moving offshore to cut taxes

for.name: Sen. Evan Bayh
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action or floor consideration; the bill sat referred to Finance until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup ever formed on it.

industries.note: The bill would tax these companies as domestic corporations, erasing the tax savings of keeping their business and shareholders in the U.S. while paying taxes as a foreign paper company. Their tax savings came at the expense of other taxpayers, so their interest ran against the public's.
The bill raises the immediate equipment write-off to $75,000 with a $325,000 phaseout through 2007, a modest tax cut for smaller firms.
